ot1.intro: Legal's Mate: White seems to give away the queen, but if Black grabs it, the bishop checks on f7 and a knight mates on d5.
notes: e4 opens the game and frees the light-squared bishop.
e5 meets White in the centre. Nothing is wrong yet, but the dark-squared bishop is about to be shut in.
Nf3 develops the king's knight and attacks the pawn on e5. This is the knight Black will pin.
d6 defends the pawn on e5 and shuts the dark-squared bishop in. That passive pawn is the first loose thread.
Bc4 aims the light-squared bishop at the pawn on f7. That is the square the combination uses.
Bg4 pins the knight on f3 to the queen on d1. Black is counting on that pin to keep the queen safe.
Nc3 develops the queen's knight. It is not the pinned piece, and it is the knight that delivers mate.
g6 spends a move on the kingside and leaves the pin on the knight on f3 untouched. The bishop on c4 still attacks the pawn on f7.
Nxe5 moves the pinned knight and takes the pawn on e5. The queen looks lost, and that is the trap.
Bxd1 takes the queen on d1. That greedy capture pulls the bishop off the pin.
Bxf7+ takes the pawn on f7 and gives check. The king is left with a single square.
Ke7 is the only legal move. The king steps to the square the queen's knight wants for the mate.
Nd5# is checkmate. The knight is protected by the bishop on f7, and the king on e7 has no flight.

ot2.intro: The Fishing Pole: Black parks a knight beside the castled king, and if White takes it the h-file opens for the queen.
notes: e4 opens the game and frees the light-squared bishop.
e5 meets White in the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop. Black is content to see a bishop come to the queenside, because the attack will be on the other wing.
Nf3 develops the king's knight and attacks the pawn on e5.
Nc6 develops the queen's knight and defends the pawn on e5. This is the knight the light-squared bishop comes to attack.
Bb5 attacks the knight on c6. The pawn on d7 still stands between that knight and the king, so this is pressure, not yet a full pin.
Nf6 develops the king's knight and attacks the pawn on e4. The trap has not started.
O-O brings the king to g1 and the rook to f1. Castling kingside puts the king where the h-file can open in front of it.
Ng4 jumps beside the castled king. It looks loose, and it is bait.
h3 attacks the knight on g4 and asks it to move. Taking is the mistake the trap is built on.
h5 supports the knight on g4. If White takes, this pawn takes back and the h-file opens.
hxg4 takes the knight on g4 and opens White's own h-file. That is the error.
hxg4 recaptures the pawn on g4 and clears the h-file. The file in front of the king on g1 is now open.
c3 is a quiet pawn move, and it leaves the open h-file alone.
a6 attacks the bishop on b5 and asks it to step away. The attack on the king is the real story.
Ba4 steps the light-squared bishop off the pawn on a6 and keeps it. The bishop is no longer the point of the position.
gxf3 takes the knight on f3 and clears the queen's road to the h-file.
Qxf3 recaptures the pawn on f3. The queen leaves d1, and the h-file stays open.
Qh4 puts the queen on the open h-file. That is the point of letting the h-file open.

ot3.intro: The Elephant Trap: a capture on d5 lets Black pin the queen, and the bishop that took the queen does not get away.
notes: d4 claims the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop.
d5 meets White in the centre. Black will keep a solid pawn here and spring the trap from a pin.
c4 attacks the pawn on d5 and offers the queen's pawn.
e6 backs up the pawn on d5 and frees the dark-squared bishop. The light-squared bishop stays inside the chain, which is normal here.
Nc3 develops the queen's knight and attacks the pawn on d5. This knight is the one that will later take, and hang the queen.
Nf6 develops the king's knight and defends the pawn on d5.
Bg5 pins the knight on f6 to the queen on d8. The whole trap is built on this pin.
Nbd7 develops the queen's knight and defends the knight on f6, so the pin does not cost a piece.
cxd5 takes the pawn on d5 and opens the c-file. The position is still normal.
exd5 recaptures the pawn on d5 and keeps a pawn in the centre. The e-file opens.
Nxd5 takes the pawn on d5. It looks like a simple capture, and it lets Black's dark-squared bishop come out against the uncastled king.
Nxd5 recaptures the knight on d5. White can take the queen, and that is the bait.
Bxd8 takes the queen on d8. It looks like the queen has been won, and the bishop has left the pin.
Bb4+ gives check along the diagonal to the king on e1. White has to answer before enjoying that queen.
Qd2 blocks the check and steps onto the pin. The bishop on b4 now pins the queen to the king on e1.
Kxd8 takes the bishop on d8. The queen on d2 is still pinned to the king, so it cannot step away.

ot4.intro: The Lasker Trap: taking the bishop lets a pawn promote to a knight with check, and the queen is lost.
notes: d4 claims the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop.
d5 meets White in the centre. Black will offer the e-pawn rather than simply hold the pawn here.
c4 attacks the pawn on d5 and offers the queen's pawn.
e5 offers the pawn so Black can plant one on d4. Giving up the pawn on e5 is the price of that central pawn.
dxe5 takes the pawn on e5 and accepts the offer.
d4 plants a pawn in the centre. That was the point of giving up the e-pawn.
e3 attacks the pawn on d4. Taking is natural, and it is what the trap wants.
Bb4+ gives check and brings the dark-squared bishop out with tempo, before the centre pawn is taken.
Bd2 blocks the check. The dark-squared bishop also stands where it can take on b4.
dxe3 takes the pawn on e3. The pawn now attacks f2, which is where the combination starts.
Bxb4 takes the bishop on b4. It looks like a free piece, and it gives Black the tempo for the pawn check.
exf2+ takes the pawn on f2 and gives check. The pawn is one square from promoting.
Ke2 steps out of check and stands next to the pawn on f2, rather than taking it.
fxg1=N+ promotes to a knight and gives check. A queen promotion would not check the king on e2, and the knight does.
Rxg1 takes the checking knight. The king had other squares, and taking here lets the bishop come in next.
Bg4+ gives check. The light-squared bishop attacks the king on e2, with the queen on d1 still at home.
Ke3 steps out of check and forward to e3. The king still cannot reach d1, and the bishop on g4 covers that square.
Qxd1 takes the queen on d1. The bishop on g4 covers the queen, so the king on e3 cannot recapture.

ot5.intro: The Blackburne Shilling Trap: a second greedy capture lets the queen take on g2 and hit the bishop.
notes: e4 opens the game and frees the light-squared bishop.
e5 meets White in the centre. The shilling trap needs this open game.
Nf3 develops the king's knight and attacks the pawn on e5.
Nc6 develops the queen's knight and defends the pawn on e5.
Bc4 aims the light-squared bishop at the pawn on f7, the square White is invited to grab.
Nd4 jumps into the centre and attacks the pawn on c2. It looks crude, and it is the trap.
Nxe5 takes the pawn on e5, the first greedy capture. The queen is about to come out.
Qg5 attacks the pawn on g2 and the knight on e5. White should step back, and grabbing again is the mistake.
Nxf7 takes the pawn on f7 and attacks the queen on g5. It looks like a fork, and the queen simply takes on g2.
Qxg2 takes the pawn on g2 and attacks the rook on h1. The queen is inside White's position.
d3 opens a diagonal for the dark-squared bishop and does not throw the queen out. The king is still on e1.
d5 attacks the bishop on c4 and frees the dark-squared bishop. The queen on g2 is already deep in White's camp.

ot6.intro: The Stafford Trap: taking the queen is the bait, and the two bishops mate the king on e2.
notes: e4 opens the game and frees the light-squared bishop.
e5 meets White in the centre. Black needs this open king's pawn game for the coming knight offer.
Nf3 develops the king's knight and attacks the pawn on e5.
Nf6 develops the king's knight and attacks the pawn on e4. Black is offering the e-pawn.
Nxe5 takes the pawn on e5 and accepts the offer. Black's queen's knight will kick this piece.
Nc6 develops the queen's knight and attacks the knight on e5.
Nxc6 takes the knight on c6. It looks like a simple trade, and Black's d-pawn takes back.
dxc6 recaptures the knight on c6 and opens the d-file. The queen's diagonal is also clearer.
d3 opens a path for the dark-squared bishop and keeps the centre modest. It does not stop what is coming.
Bc5 aims the dark-squared bishop at the pawn on f2. That is the checking piece of the mate.
Bg5 pins the knight on f6 to the queen on d8. Black is about to move that knight anyway.
Nxe4 moves the knight and takes the pawn on e4. The queen looks free to take, and that is the bait.
Bxd8 takes the queen on d8. It looks like White has won the queen, and the king is about to be mated.
Bxf2+ takes the pawn on f2 and gives check. The king is left with a single square.
Ke2 is the only legal move. The king steps out of check and beside the bishop on f2.
Bg4# is checkmate. The light-squared bishop checks the king on e2, with the other bishop already on f2.

ot7.intro: The Englund Trap: taking the bishop lets the queen finish a raid on the queenside and come away with a piece for a pawn.
notes: d4 claims the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop.
e5 offers a pawn straight away. This is a gambit, not a solid centre.
dxe5 takes the pawn on e5 and accepts the gambit.
Nc6 develops the queen's knight and attacks the pawn on e5. Black wants the queen out next, not a quiet recapture.
Nf3 develops the king's knight and defends the pawn on e5.
Qe7 develops the queen and attacks the pawn on e5 again. The queen is also ready to swing to the queenside.
Bf4 develops the dark-squared bishop and defends the pawn on e5. The bishop will be dragged off this diagonal.
Qb4+ gives check and starts the raid. The queen attacks along the fourth rank and the diagonal to the king.
Bd2 blocks the check. The dark-squared bishop leaves f4, and the pawn on b2 is now loose.
Qxb2 takes the pawn on b2. The queen is inside White's position, and the bishop on d2 is the next target.
Bc3 attacks the queen on b2. The bishop now stands where Black's dark-squared bishop can pin it.
Bb4 pins the bishop on c3 to the king on e1. Taking that bishop is the mistake the raid wants.
Bxb4 takes the bishop on b4. It looks like a trade of bishops, and it opens the way for the knight.
Nxb4 recaptures the bishop on b4. The knight replaces the bishop, and the queen's raid continues.
Na3 develops the queen's knight onto a square the queen on b2 already attacks.
Qxa3 takes the knight on a3. That is the end of the raid: the queen has collected the piece White just put there.

ot8.intro: In the Queen's Gambit Accepted, holding the extra pawn on the queenside lets the queen take the rook on a8.
notes: d4 claims the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop.
d5 meets the centre. Black will accept the gambit pawn, which this trap needs.
c4 attacks the pawn on d5 and offers the queen's pawn.
dxc4 takes the pawn on c4 and accepts the gambit. The trap is the later capture that opens the a-file, not this one.
e3 frees the light-squared bishop, which can now see the pawn on c4.
b5 holds the pawn on c4 and gains space. It also puts a pawn where White can open the a-file.
a4 attacks the pawn on b5 and asks Black how the extra pawn will be kept.
c6 backs up the pawn on b5. It looks solid, and it is the move that lets the a-file open.
axb5 takes the pawn on b5 and opens the a-file.
cxb5 recaptures the pawn on b5. The rook on a8 is now the target.
Qf3 develops the queen onto the diagonal of the rook on a8. The b-pawn has left b7, so that diagonal is clear.
a6 defends the pawn on b5 and does not block the queen. The rook on a8 stays on the diagonal.
Qxa8 takes the rook on a8. The queen was already looking down that diagonal from f3.

ot9.intro: The Damiano Defence: defending the e-pawn with the f-pawn lets the queen check at once and keep the attack going.
notes: e4 opens the game and frees the light-squared bishop.
e5 meets White in the centre. The mistake is the pawn move that follows, not this one.
Nf3 develops the king's knight and attacks the pawn on e5.
f6 tries to defend the pawn on e5 and opens the king's diagonal. That pawn move is the mistake.
Nxe5 takes the pawn on e5 and offers the knight. If Black takes it, the queen comes out along the diagonal to the king.
fxe5 takes the knight on e5. The diagonal to the king opened when the f-pawn left home, and the pawn on e5 is now a target.
Qh5+ gives check on the diagonal the f-pawn opened. If the g-pawn steps up, the queen can take on e5 and fork the king and the rook on h8.
Ke7 steps out of check. The king is in the centre, and the queen can take the pawn on e5 next.
Qxe5+ takes the pawn on e5 and gives check. The queen sits in the middle of the board beside the king.
Kf7 steps out of check again. The king is walking towards the bishop's diagonal.
Bc4+ gives check. The light-squared bishop joins the queen against the king on f7.
d5 blocks the check and attacks the bishop on c4. White simply takes.
Bxd5+ takes the pawn on d5 and gives check. The bishop stays on the diagonal of the king.
Kg6 steps out of check to g6. The king is still in the open, and the queen can check along the g-file.
Qg3+ gives check along the file to the king on g6. The queen and the bishop on d5 keep the attack going.

ot10.intro: The Kieninger Trap: taking the bishop on b4 walks into mate.
notes: d4 claims the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop.
Nf6 develops the king's knight and prepares a pawn offer.
c4 gains space and offers a queen's-pawn game. Black answers with the gambit.
e5 offers a pawn to open lines for a quick attack.
dxe5 takes the pawn on e5 and accepts the gambit.
Ng4 attacks the pawn on e5. Black wants that pawn back, or the attack that follows if White holds it.
Bf4 develops the dark-squared bishop and defends the pawn on e5.
Nc6 develops the queen's knight and attacks the pawn on e5 again.
Nf3 develops the king's knight and defends the pawn on e5. The queenside is where White is about to be careless.
Bb4+ gives check. In this trap White blocks with the queen's knight.
Nbd2 blocks the check. The queen's knight stands on the diagonal of the bishop on b4.
Qe7 develops the queen onto the e-file, where she will later pin the pawn in front of the king.
a3 attacks the bishop on b4 and asks it to move or be taken. Taking is the mistake.
Ngxe5 takes the pawn on e5 with the knight from g4. The knight is heading for the mating square.
axb4 takes the bishop on b4. Removing that bishop is the move that allows mate.
Nd3# is checkmate. The knight checks the king on e1, and the pawn on e2 cannot take it because the queen on e7 pins that pawn.

ckb1.intro: The Advance: bring the light-squared bishop out before the e-pawn closes the centre, then chip at d4 and trade White's light-squared bishop.
notes: e4 opens the game and frees the light-squared bishop.
c6 prepares a pawn in the centre and leaves the light-squared bishop free.
d4 claims the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop. The pawn on c6 is there to support Black's answer.
d5 challenges the pawn on e4 and fights for the centre. The light-squared bishop is still free, because the c-pawn moved first.
e5 gains space and clamps the centre. Black has to challenge this pawn chain before the space becomes a problem.
Bf5 develops the light-squared bishop outside the chain, before the e-pawn shuts it in. That is why the c-pawn moved first.
Nf3 develops the king's knight and defends the pawn on d4. The bishop on f5 is the piece White would like to bother.
e6 builds the pawn chain and frees the dark-squared bishop. The light-squared bishop is already on f5, so this does not shut it in.
Be2 develops the light-squared bishop and lets the king castle. Once the knight on f3 steps away, this bishop can be traded.
c5 hits the pawn on d4, the base of the chain. The pawn on e5 stays advanced, and this is how Black fights the space.
O-O brings the king to g1 and the rook to f1. The king leaves the centre before the c-file opens.
Nc6 develops the queen's knight and attacks the pawn on d4. The pawn on c5 and this knight both press the centre.
c3 supports the pawn on d4. White keeps the centre intact rather than letting the file open at once.
cxd4 takes the pawn on d4 and opens the c-file.
cxd4 recaptures the pawn on d4 and keeps a pawn in the centre. The c-file is now open.
Nge7 develops the king's knight towards the centre. It moves on before the dark-squared bishop needs this square.
Nc3 develops the queen's knight and attacks the pawn on d5.
Bg4 puts the light-squared bishop opposite the bishop on e2. The knight on f3 is in the way, and once it moves the trade is there.
Ne1 steps the king's knight off the bishop on g4. The queen's knight can then take back on e2.
Bxe2 takes the light-squared bishop on e2. That trade was the point of putting the bishop on g4.
Nxe2 recaptures the bishop on e2. The king's knight stepped aside so this knight could take.
Nf5 plants the knight where it attacks the pawn on d4. The centre is now under real pressure.
Be3 develops the dark-squared bishop and defends the pawn on d4 against the knight on f5.
Be7 develops the dark-squared bishop and prepares castling. The knight on f5 still attacks the pawn on d4 and the bishop on e3.

ckb2.intro: The main Classical: the light-squared bishop goes to f5, steps back when the h-pawn arrives, and is traded. Black then sits in a compact shell.
notes: e4 opens the game and frees the light-squared bishop.
c6 prepares a pawn in the centre and leaves the light-squared bishop free.
d4 claims the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop. The pawn on c6 is there to support Black's answer.
d5 challenges the pawn on e4 and fights for the centre. The light-squared bishop is still free, because the c-pawn moved first.
Nc3 develops the queen's knight and attacks the pawn on d5.
dxe4 takes the pawn on e4 and opens the centre. The light-squared bishop can still come out before the e-pawn moves.
Nxe4 recaptures the pawn on e4. The knight lands in the centre, where Black can develop against it.
Bf5 develops the light-squared bishop to an active square before the e-pawn moves. The bishop also attacks the knight on e4.
Ng3 attacks the bishop on f5 and asks it to drop back. White wants that bishop off the diagonal outside the pawn chain.
Bg6 keeps the light-squared bishop and steps off the knight. The bishop stays outside the pawn chain.
h4 gains space against the bishop on g6. The h-pawn is coming to kick it.
h6 gives the bishop on g6 a retreat before White's pawn arrives. The bishop will drop behind this pawn rather than get shut in.
Nf3 develops the king's knight. The h-pawn, not this knight, is the one chasing the bishop.
Nd7 develops the queen's knight and supports the king's knight coming out. Black stays flexible.
h5 kicks the bishop on g6 and gains space on the kingside. The retreat was prepared.
Bh7 tucks the light-squared bishop away from the pawn on h5. It is safe in the corner and still on the board.
Bd3 offers a trade of the bishop on h7. White would rather remove it than leave it sitting there.
Bxd3 takes the bishop on d3. Black is content to trade the light-squared bishop once it has done its job.
Qxd3 recaptures the bishop on d3. The queen's diagonal runs towards the kingside, so White's king will castle the other way.
e6 closes the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop. The light-squared bishop has already been traded, so this does not shut a piece in.
Bd2 develops the dark-squared bishop and clears the way to castle queenside.
Ngf6 develops the king's knight towards the centre. The knight on d7 is already out, so the king's knight can use this square.
O-O-O brings the king to c1 and the rook to d1. The queen on d3 looks towards the kingside, so the king goes the other way.
Be7 develops the dark-squared bishop and prepares short castling. The king will sit on the opposite wing from the king on c1.

ckb3.intro: The Exchange: with the bishop on d3, Black develops, pins the king's knight, covers the b-pawn, and trades the dark-squared bishops.
notes: e4 opens the game and frees the light-squared bishop.
c6 prepares a pawn in the centre and leaves the light-squared bishop free.
d4 claims the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop. The pawn on c6 is there to support Black's answer.
d5 challenges the pawn on e4 and fights for the centre. The light-squared bishop is still free, because the c-pawn moved first.
exd5 takes the pawn on d5 and opens the centre. Black takes back with the c-pawn.
cxd5 recaptures the pawn on d5 and opens the c-file. Black has a pawn in the centre.
Bd3 develops the light-squared bishop onto an active diagonal and attacks the pawn on h7. Black develops around this bishop.
Nc6 develops the queen's knight and attacks the pawn on d4. The c-pawn has left, so this is the knight's square.
c3 supports the pawn on d4 and blunts the knight on c6. White keeps a solid pawn centre.
Nf6 develops the king's knight and prepares castling. The centre is quiet enough to bring pieces out.
Bf4 develops the dark-squared bishop outside the pawn chain and bears on e5. That square stays under this bishop.
Bg4 develops the light-squared bishop and gets ready to pin the king's knight. Trading that knight is the idea.
Qb3 attacks the pawn on b7. Black should cover that pawn before chasing anything else.
Qd7 defends the pawn on b7 and links the queen with the dark-squared bishop. The bishop on g4 can deal with the king's knight when it arrives.
Nd2 develops the queen's knight and supports the centre. The king's knight is still free to come to f3.
e6 supports the pawn on d5 and frees the dark-squared bishop. The light-squared bishop is already on g4.
Ngf3 develops the king's knight into the path of the bishop on g4. Black is ready to take it.
Bxf3 takes the knight on f3. Giving up the bishop removes the king's knight, which is the trade this line wants.
Nxf3 recaptures the bishop on f3. White keeps the pawn structure intact by taking with the knight.
Bd6 offers a trade of dark-squared bishops and aims at the centre.
Bxd6 takes the bishop on d6. White accepts the trade.
Qxd6 recaptures the bishop on d6. The queen is developed, and the dark-squared bishops are gone.
O-O brings the king to g1 and the rook to f1. The centre is calm enough to castle.
O-O brings the king to g8 and the rook to f8. Both kings are castled, and the centre is closed and quiet.

ckb4.intro: The Panov: take back on d5 with the knight, castle, and keep that knight in front of the queen's pawn.
notes: e4 opens the game and frees the light-squared bishop.
c6 prepares a pawn in the centre and leaves the light-squared bishop free.
d4 claims the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop. The pawn on c6 is there to support Black's answer.
d5 challenges the pawn on e4 and fights for the centre. The light-squared bishop is still free, because the c-pawn moved first.
exd5 takes the pawn on d5 and opens the centre. Black takes back with the c-pawn.
cxd5 recaptures the pawn on d5 and opens the c-file. Black has a pawn in the centre.
c4 attacks the pawn on d5 and offers the Panov.
Nf6 develops the king's knight and defends the pawn on d5.
Nc3 develops the queen's knight and attacks the pawn on d5 again.
e6 supports the pawn on d5 and frees the dark-squared bishop. Black accepts the light-squared bishop inside the chain in return for a knight in the centre.
Nf3 develops the king's knight and prepares castling. The pawn on d5 is already under fire from the pawn on c4 and the knight on c3.
Be7 develops the dark-squared bishop and prepares castling. It can drop back later to help hold the centre.
cxd5 takes the pawn on d5. The knight can recapture and sit in the centre.
Nxd5 recaptures the pawn on d5 and plants a knight in the centre.
Bd3 develops the light-squared bishop towards the kingside. The knight on d5 stands in front of the queen's pawn.
Nc6 develops the queen's knight and attacks the pawn on d4. The knight on d5 stays in front of that pawn.
O-O brings the king to g1 and the rook to f1. The king gets out before Black finishes the blockade.
O-O brings the king to g8 and the rook to f8. The king is safe, and the knight on d5 stays in the centre.
Re1 puts the rook on the half-open e-file and attacks the pawn on e6.
Bf6 drops the dark-squared bishop onto the long diagonal, where it attacks the pawn on d4. The knight on d5 stays in front of that pawn.
Be4 improves the light-squared bishop and attacks the knight on d5. Black should reinforce that knight.
Nce7 brings the other knight across to defend the knight on d5.
Qd3 lines the queen up behind the bishop on e4. The bishop already attacks the pawn on h7, so Black takes a moment on the kingside.
h6 stops a knight landing on g5 and gives the king air. The bishop on e4 is the piece looking at the kingside.

ckb5.intro: The Two Knights: give up the light-squared bishop for the knight on f3, keep a solid centre, and trade the knights on e4.
notes: e4 opens the game and frees the light-squared bishop.
c6 prepares a pawn in the centre and leaves the light-squared bishop free.
Nc3 develops the queen's knight before the d-pawn joins in.
d5 challenges the pawn on e4. The knight on c3 already attacks this pawn, so the centre is a fight at once.
Nf3 develops the king's knight. Black can pin it straight away.
Bg4 pins the knight on f3 to the queen on d1. The pin is the idea of this line.
h3 asks the bishop on g4 whether it will take or retreat. Black is ready to give the bishop up.
Bxf3 takes the knight on f3. The bishop goes for the knight, which is the trade this line chooses.
Qxf3 recaptures the bishop on f3. The queen is out early, and Black builds a solid centre against her.
e6 supports the pawn on d5 and frees the dark-squared bishop. The light-squared bishop has already been traded.
Be2 develops the light-squared bishop and prepares castling. The queen on f3 is already developed.
Nf6 develops the king's knight and attacks the pawn on e4.
O-O brings the king to g1 and the rook to f1. The queen is already on f3, so the king leaves the centre before it opens.
Nbd7 develops the queen's knight and supports the knight on f6. Black is ready to take on e4 once White plays in the centre.
d4 claims the centre at last. The queen's pawn arrives after both knights are out.
dxe4 takes the pawn on e4 and opens the centre. Black wants the knight on c3 to recapture, then to trade it.
Nxe4 recaptures the pawn on e4. The knight stands in the centre, and Black can trade it off.
Nxe4 takes the knight on e4. Trading knights keeps Black's position compact.
Qxe4 recaptures the knight on e4. The queen returns to the centre.
Nf6 attacks the queen on e4 and brings the knight back into the game. The queen should step aside.
Qd3 steps the queen off the knight and stays near the centre.
Be7 develops the dark-squared bishop and prepares castling.
c4 gains space and puts a pawn beside d4. Black can castle into a compact shell.
O-O brings the king to g8 and the rook to f8. The king is safe, and the centre can be challenged next.

ckb6.intro: The Karpov Classical: the knight goes to d7 and the bishop to d6, then the queen comes to c7 and the c-pawn breaks the centre. The knight recaptures on c5.
notes: e4 opens the game and frees the light-squared bishop.
c6 prepares a pawn in the centre and leaves the light-squared bishop free.
d4 claims the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop. The pawn on c6 is there to support Black's answer.
d5 challenges the pawn on e4 and fights for the centre. The light-squared bishop is still free, because the c-pawn moved first.
Nc3 develops the queen's knight and attacks the pawn on d5.
dxe4 takes the pawn on e4 and opens the centre. The light-squared bishop can still come out before the e-pawn moves.
Nxe4 recaptures the pawn on e4. The knight lands in the centre, where Black can develop against it.
Nd7 is the Karpov move. The knight supports the king's knight and leaves the light-squared bishop flexible.
Ng5 is a nuisance jump near the king's knight's square. Black develops there anyway.
Ngf6 develops the king's knight. The knight on d7 backs it up, and White's knight on g5 is eyeing the pawn on f7.
Bd3 develops the light-squared bishop towards the kingside. Black will blunt it with a pawn and then a bishop.
e6 frees the dark-squared bishop and takes the e6 square away from the knight on g5.
N1f3 brings the other knight out and prepares castling. The knight on g5 is the one making the nuisance.
Bd6 develops the dark-squared bishop onto an active diagonal, aimed at the centre.
Qe2 develops the queen onto the e-file. White keeps the choice of which side to castle.
h6 asks the knight on g5 a question before Black castles. It should not be left sitting there.
Ne4 drops the knight back from g5 onto a central square. Black can trade it.
Nxe4 takes the knight on e4. Black removes the knight that dropped back into the centre.
Qxe4 recaptures the knight on e4. The queen looks towards h7, with the bishop on d3 sitting behind her.
Qc7 develops the queen and defends the bishop on d6. The queen also defends the pawn on c6, ready for the c-pawn to challenge the pawn on d4.
Bd2 develops the dark-squared bishop and attacks the pawn on h6. The bishop also clears the back rank so the king can castle long.
c5 attacks the pawn on d4 and breaks the centre. The queen on c7 stands behind the break.
dxc5 takes the pawn on c5 and attacks the bishop on d6. White opens the centre.
Nxc5 recaptures the pawn on c5 and attacks the bishop on d3. The knight also attacks the queen on e4.
Bb5+ gives check and attacks the king on e8.
Bd7 blocks the check and attacks the bishop on b5. The light-squared bishop comes out in front of the king on e8.

ckb7.intro: The Fantasy: the knight steps into a pin on e5, the bishop takes the queen, and Black's queen comes out with check.
notes: e4 opens the game and frees the light-squared bishop.
c6 prepares a pawn in the centre and leaves the light-squared bishop free.
d4 claims the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop. The pawn on c6 is there to support Black's answer.
d5 challenges the pawn on e4 and fights for the centre. The light-squared bishop is still free, because the c-pawn moved first.
f3 is the Fantasy. It supports the pawn on e4 and blocks the king's knight, which is the drawback Black can use.
dxe4 takes the pawn on e4 and opens the centre. Black is happy to see the f-pawn recapture.
fxe4 recaptures the pawn on e4 and opens the f-file. The king's knight still has no natural square.
e5 attacks the pawn on d4 and offers a pawn. If the knight comes to f3, the bishop to g4 pins it, and taking on e5 then loses the queen.
Nf3 develops the king's knight onto the square the pin wants, and it attacks the pawn on e5.
Bg4 pins the knight on f3 to the queen on d1. Taking the pawn now loses the queen.
Nxe5 moves the pinned knight and takes the pawn on e5. The queen looks free, and that is the mistake.
Bxd1 takes the queen on d1. The pin was real, and the queen comes off.
Kxd1 takes the bishop on d1. The king steps into the centre to collect the bishop, and it can no longer castle.
Qxd4+ takes the pawn on d4 and gives check. The queen comes out while the king stands on d1.
Nd3 blocks the check by stepping in front of the king. The knight on d3 is now a target.
Nf6 develops the king's knight and attacks the pawn on e4.
Nd2 brings the queen's knight out beside the king on d1. The king still needs a safer square.
Qd8 steps the queen back from d4. The check has done its job, and the queen stays out of trouble.
c3 opens a path for the king towards the queenside and supports the centre.
Nbd7 develops the queen's knight towards the centre.
Kc2 walks the king towards the queenside. The king has already moved, so castling is no longer possible.
Nc5 attacks the knight on d3 and the pawn on e4. The knight joins the pressure on White's centre.
a4 gains a little space on the queenside. It does not replace the queen.
Qd7 brings the queen out again. The knights are already on f6 and c5.

ckb8.intro: Classical with the knight on f6: take back with the e-pawn, castle, and put a rook on the open e-file.
notes: e4 opens the game and frees the light-squared bishop.
c6 prepares a pawn in the centre and leaves the light-squared bishop free.
d4 claims the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop. The pawn on c6 is there to support Black's answer.
d5 challenges the pawn on e4 and fights for the centre. The light-squared bishop is still free, because the c-pawn moved first.
Nc3 develops the queen's knight and attacks the pawn on d5.
dxe4 takes the pawn on e4 and opens the centre. The light-squared bishop can still come out before the e-pawn moves.
Nxe4 recaptures the pawn on e4. The knight lands in the centre, where Black can develop against it.
Nf6 attacks the knight on e4. Black offers the trade that will shape the pawn structure.
Nxf6+ takes the knight on f6 and gives check. Black chooses how to recapture, and the e-pawn is the solid choice.
exf6 recaptures the knight on f6 and opens the e-file. The pawn on f6 keeps the kingside compact.
Nf3 develops the king's knight and prepares castling.
Bd6 develops the dark-squared bishop onto an active diagonal. The light-squared bishop can come out afterwards.
Bd3 develops the light-squared bishop opposite the bishop on d6. White points a piece at the kingside.
O-O brings the king to g8 and the rook to f8. The king is safe behind the pawn on f6.
O-O brings the king to g1 and the rook to f1, stepping off the open e-file.
Re8 puts the rook on the open e-file. That was the point of recapturing with the e-pawn.
c3 supports the pawn on d4 and keeps the centre solid.
Nd7 develops the queen's knight. It can head for the centre or the kingside without a rushed pawn break.

ckb9.intro: Another Advance: hit the base of the pawn chain early, pin the king's knight, open the c-file, and bring the other knight towards the centre.
notes: e4 opens the game and frees the light-squared bishop.
c6 prepares a pawn in the centre and leaves the light-squared bishop free.
d4 claims the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop. The pawn on c6 is there to support Black's answer.
d5 challenges the pawn on e4 and fights for the centre. The light-squared bishop is still free, because the c-pawn moved first.
e5 gains space and clamps the centre. Black has to challenge this pawn chain before the space becomes a problem.
c5 hits the pawn on d4 at once, before the light-squared bishop comes out. This move order attacks the base of the chain immediately.
c3 supports the pawn on d4 and keeps the chain intact.
Nc6 develops the queen's knight and attacks the pawn on d4.
Nf3 develops the king's knight and defends the pawn on d4. The knight can be pinned.
Bg4 pins the knight on f3 to the queen on d1. The pin adds to the pressure on the pawn on d4.
Be2 develops the light-squared bishop and blocks the pin, so the knight on f3 is no longer pinned to the queen.
e6 builds the chain and frees the dark-squared bishop. The light-squared bishop is already active on g4.
O-O brings the king to g1 and the rook to f1. The king leaves before the centre opens.
cxd4 takes the pawn on d4 and opens the c-file against White's position.
cxd4 recaptures the pawn on d4 and restores a pawn in the centre. The c-file stays open.
Nge7 develops the king's knight towards the centre.

ckb10.intro: The Panov with a fianchetto: castle, then the queen's knight asks the bishop on c4 to move.
notes: e4 opens the game and frees the light-squared bishop.
c6 prepares a pawn in the centre and leaves the light-squared bishop free.
d4 claims the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop. The pawn on c6 is there to support Black's answer.
d5 challenges the pawn on e4 and fights for the centre. The light-squared bishop is still free, because the c-pawn moved first.
exd5 takes the pawn on d5 and opens the centre. Black takes back with the c-pawn.
cxd5 recaptures the pawn on d5 and opens the c-file. Black has a pawn in the centre.
c4 attacks the pawn on d5 and offers the Panov.
Nf6 develops the king's knight and defends the pawn on d5.
Nc3 develops the queen's knight and attacks the pawn on d5 again.
g6 prepares a fianchetto. The dark-squared bishop will go to the long diagonal instead of a compact e-pawn shell.
Nf3 develops the king's knight and prepares castling. The pawn on d5 is still attacked by the pawn on c4 and the knight on c3.
Bg7 puts the dark-squared bishop on the long diagonal, behind the knight on f6. When that knight moves, the diagonal opens.
cxd5 takes the pawn on d5 and opens the centre while Black is about to castle. The recapture can wait one move.
O-O brings the king to g8 and the rook to f8. The king gets out first, and the bishop on g7 stays on its diagonal.
Bc4 develops the light-squared bishop onto an active diagonal. The queen's knight can ask this bishop to move.
Nbd7 develops the queen's knight towards the queenside.
O-O brings the king to g1 and the rook to f1. White castles before the bishop is kicked.
Nb6 attacks the bishop on c4 and asks it where it wants to go. The bishop on g7 keeps the long diagonal.

lon1.intro: The classical London pyramid: the dark-squared bishop stays out, drops to g3 against the bishop on d6, and the knight on e5 is backed up by the f-pawn.
notes: d4 claims the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop. That bishop comes out before the e-pawn moves.
d5 meets White in the centre. A closed centre is fine, and the dark-squared bishop is about to step outside the chain.
Bf4 develops the dark-squared bishop outside the pawn chain, before the e-pawn can shut it in.
Nf6 develops the king's knight. Black gets a piece out while White finishes the pyramid.
e3 supports the pawn on d4 and frees the light-squared bishop. The dark-squared bishop is already outside, so this pawn does not shut it in.
c5 hits the pawn on d4 and fights for space. White will support the centre rather than take at once.
c3 supports the pawn on d4 and builds the pyramid. The queen's knight stays off the c-file so this pawn can remain.
Nc6 develops the queen's knight and attacks the pawn on d4.
Nd2 develops the queen's knight behind the pawn on c3. The pawn stays where it supports d4.
e6 supports the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop. Black builds a solid shell of their own.
Ngf3 develops the king's knight and prepares castling. Black's dark-squared bishop will challenge White's.
Bd6 develops the dark-squared bishop and attacks White's dark-squared bishop. White should keep that bishop if possible.
Bg3 steps the dark-squared bishop off the attack and keeps it. Trading it for the bishop on d6 is not the idea.
O-O brings the king to g8 and the rook to f8. Black castles before the kingside gets clamped.
Bd3 develops the light-squared bishop and aims at the pawn on h7. The king is already on g8.
b6 prepares a fianchetto for the light-squared bishop. The bishop will sit on the long diagonal.
Ne5 plants the knight on a central outpost. The pawn on d4 supports it.
Bb7 puts the light-squared bishop on the long diagonal. The pawn on d5 stands in front of it for now.
O-O brings the king to g1 and the rook to f1. The king is safe before the kingside pawn moves.
Qc7 develops the queen and connects the rooks. She watches the centre from the queenside.
f4 supports the knight on e5 and gains space on the kingside. The pawn keeps that knight anchored.

lon2.intro: Black takes on d4 early. The centre opens, the light-squared bishop comes to f5, and the bishop on d6 hits the bishop on f4.
notes: d4 claims the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop. That bishop comes out before the e-pawn moves.
d5 meets White in the centre. A closed centre is fine, and the dark-squared bishop is about to step outside the chain.
Bf4 develops the dark-squared bishop outside the pawn chain, before the e-pawn can shut it in.
Nf6 develops the king's knight. Black gets a piece out while White finishes the pyramid.
e3 supports the pawn on d4 and frees the light-squared bishop. The dark-squared bishop is already outside, so this pawn does not shut it in.
c5 hits the pawn on d4 and fights for space. White will support the centre rather than take at once.
c3 supports the pawn on d4 and builds the pyramid. The queen's knight stays off the c-file so this pawn can remain.
Nc6 develops the queen's knight and attacks the pawn on d4.
Nd2 develops the queen's knight behind the pawn on c3. The pawn stays where it supports d4.
cxd4 takes the pawn on d4 and opens the centre. White takes back with the e-pawn.
exd4 recaptures the pawn on d4 and opens the e-file for White. Development still comes first.
Bf5 develops the light-squared bishop outside the pawn chain. With the centre open, this is the active square.
Ngf3 develops the king's knight and prepares castling.
e6 supports the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop.
Bb5 pins the knight on c6 to the king on e8. The d-pawn has already moved, so the pin is real, and the bishop develops with tempo.
Bd6 develops the dark-squared bishop and attacks the bishop on f4. That bishop is the one to deal with.

lon3.intro: An immediate hit on d4. After the centre opens, both sides develop and castle, and the queen comes to the c-file.
notes: d4 claims the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop. That bishop comes out before the e-pawn moves.
Nf6 develops the king's knight and keeps Black's options open. There is no central pawn yet.
Bf4 develops the dark-squared bishop outside the pawn chain, before the e-pawn moves.
c5 hits the pawn on d4 at once, before Black has a pawn in the centre.
e3 supports the pawn on d4 and frees the light-squared bishop. The dark-squared bishop is already out.
cxd4 takes the pawn on d4 and opens the centre.
exd4 recaptures the pawn on d4. The e-file opens, and White keeps a pawn in the centre.
d5 claims a pawn in the centre against the open position. The structure now resembles an exchange centre.
c3 supports the pawn on d4 and builds the pyramid, even with the e-file open.
Nc6 develops the queen's knight and attacks the pawn on d4.
Nd2 develops the queen's knight without blocking the pawn on c3.
Bf5 develops the light-squared bishop outside the chain. The centre is open, so this bishop wants a square.
Ngf3 develops the king's knight and prepares castling.
e6 supports the pawn on d5 and frees the dark-squared bishop.
Be2 develops the light-squared bishop and prepares castling. With the centre open, this solid square is enough.
Bd6 attacks the bishop on f4. White can step aside and keep the bishop.
Bg3 keeps the dark-squared bishop and steps off the attack from the bishop on d6.
O-O brings the king to g8 and the rook to f8. The king steps off the e-file.
O-O brings the king to g1 and the rook to f1. Both kings are out, and the c-file is Black's avenue.
Qc7 develops the queen onto the half-open c-file and connects the rooks.

lon4.intro: A king's Indian against the London. When the e-pawn advances, the dark-squared bishop drops back and stays on the board.
notes: d4 claims the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop. That bishop comes out before the e-pawn moves.
Nf6 develops the king's knight and keeps Black's options open. There is no central pawn yet.
Bf4 develops the dark-squared bishop outside the pawn chain, before the e-pawn moves.
g6 prepares a fianchetto. The dark-squared bishop wants the long diagonal.
e3 supports the centre and frees the light-squared bishop. The dark-squared bishop stays on f4, outside the chain.
Bg7 puts the dark-squared bishop on the long diagonal, behind the knight on f6.
Nf3 develops the king's knight and prepares castling.
O-O brings the king to g8 and the rook to f8. The king tucks in behind the fianchetto.
Be2 develops the light-squared bishop and prepares castling. White stays classical against this setup.
d6 keeps the centre flexible and frees the light-squared bishop. The e-pawn can still choose its moment.
h3 gives the bishop on f4 a retreat and stops a piece landing on g4. The drop back is ready before the centre opens.
Nbd7 develops the queen's knight and supports the centre. The king's knight stays on f6.
O-O brings the king to g1 and the rook to f1. The king steps off the e-file.
Qe8 slides the queen across so a central pawn push will not block her. The rook can then use the e-file.
c3 supports the pawn on d4. White wants that pawn solid when the centre opens.
e5 challenges the pawn on d4 and attacks the bishop on f4. The bishop should leave this diagonal.
Bh2 keeps the dark-squared bishop. Retreating here rather than taking keeps the bishop, and it still looks down the diagonal towards the pawn on e5.
Qe7 puts the queen on the e-file, in front of the pawn on e5. The rook can stand behind her.
Nbd2 develops the queen's knight beside the pawn on c3 and supports the centre.
Re8 puts the rook on the e-file behind the queen on e7. That file is Black's lever.

lon5.intro: An Indian move order that reaches the London pyramid. The queen goes to e2, and with the king's knight out the centre break is the e-pawn.
notes: d4 claims the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop. That bishop comes out before the e-pawn moves.
Nf6 develops the king's knight and keeps Black's options open. There is no central pawn yet.
Bf4 develops the dark-squared bishop outside the pawn chain, before the e-pawn moves.
e6 frees the dark-squared bishop and prepares a pawn centre. The d-pawn has not moved yet.
e3 supports the centre and frees the light-squared bishop. The dark-squared bishop is already on f4.
c5 hits the pawn on d4. Black fights for space before committing the d-pawn.
c3 supports the pawn on d4 and starts the pyramid.
Nc6 develops the queen's knight and attacks the pawn on d4. It also watches e5, so a white knight landing there can be taken.
Nd2 develops the queen's knight without blocking the pawn on c3.
d5 finally plants a pawn in the centre, so the pawn chain is complete.
Ngf3 develops the king's knight and prepares castling. This knight blocks a kingside pawn push, so a central break has to come from the e-pawn.
Bd6 attacks the bishop on f4.
Bg3 keeps the dark-squared bishop and steps off the bishop on d6.
O-O brings the king to g8 and the rook to f8. The king steps off the e-file.
Bd3 develops the light-squared bishop and aims at the pawn on h7.
b6 prepares the light-squared bishop's fianchetto.
O-O brings the king to g1 and the rook to f1. The king steps off the e-file.
Bb7 puts the light-squared bishop on the long diagonal. The pawn on d5 stands in front of it.
Qe2 develops the queen behind the pawn on e3, ready to support a central break. She also connects the rooks.
Qc7 develops the queen and connects the rooks. The queenside pieces are in, and the centre is the fight.

lon6.intro: The Jobava: the queen's knight goes to c3, Black takes on d4, and the light-squared bishop trades for the knight on f3.
notes: d4 claims the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop. That bishop comes out before the e-pawn moves.

Nc3 develops the queen's knight and attacks the pawn on d5. The Jobava puts the knight here and leaves the c-pawn at home.
Nf6 develops the king's knight and defends the pawn on d5.
Bf4 develops the dark-squared bishop outside the chain. Even in the Jobava, that bishop comes out before the e-pawn.
c5 hits the pawn on d4 and challenges the centre the knight is holding.
e3 supports the pawn on d4 and frees the light-squared bishop.
cxd4 takes the pawn on d4 and opens the centre.
exd4 recaptures the pawn on d4 and opens the e-file. White keeps a pawn in the centre.
a6 gains space and takes b5 away from White's pieces. The pin of the king's knight comes next.
Nf3 develops the king's knight. It can be pinned at once.
Bg4 pins the knight on f3 to the queen on d1. Black is ready to trade the bishop for that knight.
h3 asks the bishop on g4 a question. Black is ready to take.
Bxf3 takes the knight on f3. The bishop goes for the knight, and the queen takes back.
Qxf3 recaptures the bishop on f3. The queen is developed, and the centre pawn stays on d4.
e6 supports the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop. Black stays solid against the early queen.

lon7.intro: The light-squared bishop comes to f5 and the queen comes to b6. White meets that queen and gains space with the c-pawn.
notes: d4 claims the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop. That bishop comes out before the e-pawn moves.
d5 meets White in the centre. A closed centre is fine, and the dark-squared bishop is about to step outside the chain.
Bf4 develops the dark-squared bishop outside the pawn chain, before the e-pawn can shut it in.

Bf5 develops the light-squared bishop outside the chain, before the e-pawn closes. The bishop comes out while it still can.
c4 attacks the pawn on d5 and gains space. This is sharper than the quiet pyramid.
e6 supports the pawn on d5 and frees the dark-squared bishop. The light-squared bishop is already on f5.
Nc3 develops the queen's knight and attacks the pawn on d5. With the c-pawn on c4, this is the natural square.
c6 supports the pawn on d5 and keeps the centre solid.
Nf3 develops the king's knight and prepares castling.
Nbd7 develops the queen's knight and supports the centre. The queen can come out to the queenside.
Qb3 attacks the pawn on b7 and stands where Black's queen wants a fight.
Qb6 develops the queen opposite the queen on b3. A queen trade is available, and White can also push past.
c5 gains space and fixes the queenside. The queen on b3 stays opposite the queen on b6.

lon8.intro: An early queen on b6. White meets her, steps aside from the pawn wedge, and finishes developing.
notes: d4 claims the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop. That bishop comes out before the e-pawn moves.

Nc6 develops the queen's knight and attacks the pawn on d4.
Nbd2 develops the queen's knight and supports the centre. The pawn on c3 is already doing its job.
Bg4 develops the light-squared bishop and gets ready to pin the king's knight.
Ngf3 develops the king's knight into the path of the bishop on g4.
e6 supports the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop. The light-squared bishop is already on g4.

lon9.intro: A fianchetto with a pawn on d5. White takes on c5, keeps the dark-squared bishop, and tucks it away when a knight kicks it.
notes: d4 claims the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop. That bishop comes out before the e-pawn moves.
Nf6 develops the king's knight and keeps Black's options open. There is no central pawn yet.
Bf4 develops the dark-squared bishop outside the pawn chain, before the e-pawn moves.
g6 prepares a fianchetto. The dark-squared bishop wants the long diagonal.

Bg7 puts the dark-squared bishop on the long diagonal, behind the king's knight.

d5 plants a pawn in the centre. Black mixes the fianchetto with a classical pawn, rather than staying fully closed.
c3 supports the pawn on d4 and builds the pyramid.
O-O brings the king to g8 and the rook to f8, behind the bishop on g7.
Nbd2 develops the queen's knight without blocking the pawn on c3.
c5 hits the pawn on d4. White can take and still keep the dark-squared bishop.
Be2 develops the light-squared bishop and prepares castling.
Nc6 develops the queen's knight and attacks the pawn on d4.
dxc5 takes the pawn on c5. The pawns on c3 and c5 are doubled, and the bishop on f4 stays on its diagonal.

Nh5 attacks the bishop on f4 and asks it to move. Black wants that bishop off its diagonal.
Bg5 keeps the dark-squared bishop and steps off the knight on h5. The bishop stays on the board.
f6 kicks the bishop on g5. The pawn also stands in front of the bishop on g7 for the moment.
Bh4 keeps the dark-squared bishop and steps off the pawn on f6. Keeping this bishop was the point of the earlier capture.
e5 claims a pawn in the centre. The bishop on h4 remains outside the chain.

lon10.intro: A knight on c6 against the London, without an early pawn hit. Black keeps the light-squared bishop, and White asks it a question with the knight.

it1.intro: The Giuoco Pianissimo: both bishops take up active diagonals, and White keeps the centre closed with the c-pawn and the d-pawn.
notes: e4 opens the game and frees the light-squared bishop, so that bishop can take up the diagonal in front of the black king.

it2.intro: The main Two Knights: after the knight jumps towards f7, a pawn in the centre and a knight out to a5 are the sound answer. This is not the Fried Liver.
notes: e4 opens the game and frees the light-squared bishop, so that bishop can take up the diagonal in front of the black king.
e5 meets White in the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop.

it5.intro: The Fried Liver. After the knight takes on d5, White gives the knight up on f7 and follows the king out to e6.

qg9.intro: The Albin: Black plants a pawn on d4, and White fianchettoes against it, castles, and trades the knights.

Be7 develops the dark-squared bishop and prepares castling.

qg10.intro: The Moscow: White takes the knight on f6, the queen takes back, and Black prepares a fianchetto after taking on c4.

d5 meets White in the centre. Black is ready to decline or take the gambit pawn.
c4 attacks the pawn on d5. White offers a wing pawn: taking it draws the centre pawn off d5, and declining leaves the pressure on.
c6 supports the pawn on d5 and leaves the light-squared bishop free.

frb1.intro: The Winawer: the dark-squared bishop takes on c3, the queen comes to a5, and Black breaks with the c-pawn and the f-pawn before castling long.

Bd7 develops the light-squared bishop and supports the queen coming out.

frb2.intro: The Advance with the queen on b6: the knight comes via h6 to f5, and the e-pawn takes the bishop.
notes: e4 opens the game and frees the light-squared bishop.

O-O brings the king to g1 and the rook to f1. The king steps off the e-file.
Be6 develops the light-squared bishop to a solid square and completes the minor pieces.

frb3.intro: The Advance with the bishop on d7: the knight goes to g6, steps to h8 when the h-pawn arrives, and Black breaks with the f-pawn.
notes: e4 opens the game and frees the light-squared bishop.

d4 claims the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop.
d5 challenges the pawn on e4 and builds a pawn chain. The light-squared bishop stays inside that chain.
e5 gains space and clamps the centre. Black has to attack this pawn chain.
c5 attacks the pawn on d4, the base of the chain.
c3 supports the pawn on d4 and keeps the chain intact.
Nc6 develops the queen's knight and attacks the pawn on d4.
Nf3 develops the king's knight and defends the pawn on d4.
Bd7 develops the light-squared bishop and leaves the queen at home. Black keeps the queen off an early raid.
Be2 develops the light-squared bishop and prepares castling.
Nge7 develops the king's knight towards g6. The pawn on e5 has taken the usual square.
O-O brings the king to g1 and the rook to f1. The king steps off the e-file.
Ng6 brings the knight to the kingside and attacks the pawn on e5.

Bf4 develops the dark-squared bishop and holds the chain.
cxd4 takes the pawn on d4 and opens the c-file. Black times the capture after castling.
cxd4 recaptures the pawn on d4 and keeps the central pawn.
Be8 tucks the light-squared bishop back so the f-pawn can move, and it can redeploy.

f6 challenges the pawn on e5. This break hits the head of the pawn chain.
Rh1 puts the rook back on the h-file. It does not answer the break.
fxe5 takes the pawn on e5 and opens the f-file. The chain has been challenged.

frb4.intro: The open Tarrasch: both sides take back with pawns, the c-pawns come off, Black is left with an isolated pawn on d5, and the light-squared bishop comes to g4.

e6 prepares a central pawn and shuts the light-squared bishop in. Black accepts that bishop for a solid centre.

Nc6 develops the queen's knight and attacks the pawn on d4.

Bd6 drops the dark-squared bishop back and keeps it. The bishop still aims at the kingside.

frb5.intro: The closed Tarrasch: the knight drops to d7, Black breaks with the f-pawn, and the knight lands on e4 after the bishops trade.

Nxf4 recaptures the bishop on f4. The knight lands on an active square.
Ne4 plants the knight on the central outpost. That was the point of the break and the trades.

frb6.intro: The Classical: the dark-squared bishop breaks the pin, White takes it on e7, the queen takes back, and the light-squared bishop comes to b7.
notes: e4 opens the game and frees the light-squared bishop.

Bd3 develops the light-squared bishop and aims at the kingside.
b5 gains queenside space and prepares the light-squared bishop.
O-O brings the king to g1 and the rook to f1. The king steps off the e-file.
Bb7 develops the light-squared bishop on the long diagonal. The bishop finally has a square outside the pawn chain.

frb7.intro: The Steinitz: the knight drops to d7, the c-pawn hits d4, and the queen comes to b6.

Qxd8+ takes the queen on d8 and gives check. The queens come off and an endgame starts.
Kxd8 takes the queen on d8 and gets out of check. The king is in the centre, which this line accepts.
Nc3 develops the queen's knight. White gets another piece out in the queenless position.
Ke8 steps the king back towards safety. It is not castling, but it leaves the d-file.
h3 gives the king air and takes g4 away from Black's pieces.
Be6 develops the light-squared bishop to a solid square.
Rd1 puts the rook on the open d-file. The king has stepped aside to e8.
Be7 develops the dark-squared bishop and covers the king.
Ne4 plants the knight in the centre. The endgame play is about this knight and the open file.

rlw4.intro: The Open Defence: Black takes on e4, holds the centre with a pawn on d5, and White builds with the c-pawn, a knight on d2, and the bishop on c2.
notes: e4 opens the game and frees the light-squared bishop.
e5 meets White in the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop.
Nf3 develops the king's knight and attacks the pawn on e5.
Nc6 develops the queen's knight and defends the pawn on e5.
Bb5 attacks the knight on c6. The pawn on d7 still stands between that knight and the king, so this is pressure, not yet a full pin.
a6 asks the light-squared bishop a question.
Ba4 keeps the light-squared bishop. Retreating rather than taking keeps that bishop for later.
Nf6 develops the king's knight and attacks the pawn on e4.
O-O brings the king to g1 and the rook to f1. The pawn on e4 can be taken.
Nxe4 takes the pawn on e4 and attacks the pawns on d2 and f2.
d4 challenges the pawn on e5 and opens lines. White does not take the knight back at once.
b5 attacks the bishop on a4 and gains space.
Bb3 keeps the light-squared bishop on the diagonal towards the centre.
d5 plants a pawn in the centre and defends the knight on e4. The pawn also blocks the bishop on b3.
dxe5 takes the pawn on e5 and opens the centre. The knight on e4 stays for the moment.
Be6 develops the light-squared bishop and challenges the bishop on b3.
c3 supports the centre and gives the light-squared bishop a retreat.
Bc5 develops the dark-squared bishop onto an active diagonal.
Nbd2 develops the queen's knight and challenges the knight on e4.
O-O brings the king to g8 and the rook to f8. The king steps off the e-file.
Bc2 keeps the light-squared bishop and adds a second attacker on the knight on e4.
Nxd2 takes the knight on d2. Black removes the piece that was challenging the centre.
Qxd2 recaptures the knight on d2 and develops the queen.

rlw5.intro: The Exchange: White takes on c6, the queens come off, and a knight lands on c4 against the bishop on d6.
notes: e4 opens the game and frees the light-squared bishop.
e5 meets White in the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop.
Nf3 develops the king's knight and attacks the pawn on e5.
Nc6 develops the queen's knight and defends the pawn on e5.
Bb5 attacks the knight on c6. The pawn on d7 still stands between that knight and the king, so this is pressure, not yet a full pin.
a6 asks the bishop on b5 a question. In this line White takes.
Bxc6 takes the knight on c6. White gives up the bishop pair to damage Black's pawns.
dxc6 recaptures the bishop on c6 and opens the d-file. The pawns are doubled.
O-O brings the king to g1 and the rook to f1. The king steps off the e-file.
f6 supports the pawn on e5. The king's side is a little airy, which this structure accepts.
d4 opens the centre and attacks the pawn on e5.
Bg4 pins the knight on f3 to the queen on d1. The pin is real.
dxe5 takes the pawn on e5 and opens the d-file. The queens now face each other.
Qxd1 takes the queen on d1. Black is happy to trade into the endgame.
Rxd1 recaptures the queen on d1. The rook arrives on the open file.
fxe5 takes the pawn on e5 and restores a pawn in the centre.
Rd3 lifts the rook. It can swing along the third rank and keep pressure.
Bd6 develops the dark-squared bishop and defends the pawn on e5.
Nbd2 develops the queen's knight towards c4.
Nf6 develops the king's knight and attacks the pawn on e4.
Nc4 attacks the bishop on d6 and the pawn on e5. That is the square the knight was heading for.

rlw6.intro: The Schliemann: Black strikes with the f-pawn, White's knights take in the centre, and the g-pawn takes back before both sides castle.
notes: e4 opens the game and frees the light-squared bishop.
e5 meets White in the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop.
Nf3 develops the king's knight and attacks the pawn on e5.
Nc6 develops the queen's knight and defends the pawn on e5.
Bb5 attacks the knight on c6. The pawn on d7 still stands between that knight and the king, so this is pressure, not yet a full pin.
f5 is the Schliemann. Black challenges the pawn on e4 at once and accepts an open king's side.
Nc3 develops the queen's knight and defends the pawn on e4. White meets the gambit with a piece.
fxe4 takes the pawn on e4 and opens the f-file.
Nxe4 recaptures the pawn on e4. The knight stands in the centre.
Nf6 attacks the knight on e4 and develops the king's knight.
Qe2 develops the queen and defends the knight on e4.
d5 attacks the knight on e4 and claims the centre.
Nxf6+ takes the knight on f6 and gives check.
gxf6 recaptures the knight on f6 and gets out of check. One pawn stands on the f-file.
d4 opens the centre against the pawn on e5.
Bg7 puts the dark-squared bishop on the long diagonal and prepares castling.
dxe5 takes the pawn on e5 and opens lines.
O-O brings the king to g8 and the rook to f8. Black castles before the queenside is touched.
Bxc6 takes the knight on c6 and damages the queenside as well.
bxc6 recaptures the bishop on c6. The c-pawns are doubled, and the bishop on g7 stays.
O-O brings the king to g1 and the rook to f1. White castles once the tactics have settled.

rlw7.intro: The Classical with the bishop on c5: White opens the centre, the queen comes to d5, and then steps home once the knight has moved.
notes: e4 opens the game and frees the light-squared bishop.
e5 meets White in the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop.
Nf3 develops the king's knight and attacks the pawn on e5.
Nc6 develops the queen's knight and defends the pawn on e5.
Bb5 attacks the knight on c6. The pawn on d7 still stands between that knight and the king, so this is pressure, not yet a full pin.
Bc5 develops the dark-squared bishop and aims at the pawn on f2.
c3 prepares the central pawn push and takes b4 away from the bishop.
Nf6 develops the king's knight and attacks the pawn on e4.
O-O brings the king to g1 and the rook to f1. The king steps off the e-file.
O-O brings the king to g8 and the rook to f8. The king steps off the e-file.
d4 attacks the bishop on c5 and opens the centre.
Bb6 keeps the dark-squared bishop and steps off the pawn.
dxe5 takes the pawn on e5 and opens the centre. The new pawn attacks the knight on f6.
Nxe4 takes the pawn on e4. The knight jumps into the centre.
Qd5 attacks the undefended knight on e4. She also hits the knight on c6.
Nc5 steps the knight off the queen.
Bg5 develops the dark-squared bishop and attacks the queen on d8.
Ne7 steps the queen's knight in front of the queen and attacks the queen on d5.
Qd1 steps the queen off that knight and back home.

rlw8.intro: The Old Steinitz: Black plays a pawn to d6, the centre opens, and White drops the bishop back before bringing the knight to f3.
notes: e4 opens the game and frees the light-squared bishop.
e5 meets White in the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop.
Nf3 develops the king's knight and attacks the pawn on e5.
Nc6 develops the queen's knight and defends the pawn on e5.
Bb5 attacks the knight on c6. The pawn on d7 still stands between that knight and the king, so this is pressure, not yet a full pin.
d6 supports the pawn on e5 and keeps the position solid. Black accepts a slightly cramped centre.
d4 opens the centre at once. Against this passive pawn, White does not wait.
Bd7 develops the light-squared bishop and breaks the pressure on the knight on c6.
Nc3 develops the queen's knight and supports the centre.
Nf6 develops the king's knight and attacks the pawn on e4.
O-O brings the king to g1 and the rook to f1. The king steps off the e-file.
Be7 develops the dark-squared bishop and prepares castling.
Re1 puts the rook on the e-file.
exd4 takes the pawn on d4 and releases the centre.
Nxd4 recaptures the pawn on d4 and puts a knight in the centre.
O-O brings the king to g8 and the rook to f8. The king steps off the e-file.
Bf1 brings the light-squared bishop home. White keeps it rather than trade it on c6.
Re8 puts the rook on the e-file.
Nf3 brings the knight back from d4, and the queen on d1 looks up the file at the pawn on d6.

rlw9.intro: The Bird Defence: the knight jumps to d4, White takes and castles, and the bishop comes to c4 before the centre is settled.
notes: e4 opens the game and frees the light-squared bishop.
e5 meets White in the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop.
Nf3 develops the king's knight and attacks the pawn on e5.
Nc6 develops the queen's knight and defends the pawn on e5.
Bb5 attacks the queen's knight. The pawn on d7 still stands between that knight and the king, so this is pressure, not yet a full pin.

Nxd4 takes the knight on d4. White removes the jumper rather than moving the bishop.
exd4 recaptures the knight on d4. Black has a pawn in the centre.
O-O brings the king to g1 and the rook to f1. The king leaves before that pawn becomes a problem.
c6 attacks the bishop on b5 and asks it to move.
Bc4 steps the light-squared bishop off the pawn and aims at the pawn on f7.
Nf6 develops the king's knight and attacks the pawn on e4.
Re1 puts the rook behind the pawn on e4.
d6 frees the light-squared bishop and keeps a pawn in the centre.

Be7 develops the dark-squared bishop and prepares castling.
cxd4 takes the pawn on d4 and removes the wedge.
O-O brings the king to g8 and the rook to f8. The king steps off the e-file.
d3 supports the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop. The position has settled into a normal open game.

rlw10.intro: The Marshall Gambit: Black gives a pawn for an attack, the queen comes to the kingside, and White meets it with the g-pawn, the bishop, and the queen.
notes: e4 opens the game and frees the light-squared bishop.
e5 meets White in the centre and frees the dark-squared bishop.
Nf3 develops the king's knight and attacks the pawn on e5.
Nc6 develops the queen's knight and defends the pawn on e5.
Bb5 attacks the queen's knight. The pawn on d7 still stands between that knight and the king, so this is pressure, not yet a full pin.
a6 asks the light-squared bishop a question.
Ba4 keeps the light-squared bishop. Retreating rather than taking keeps that bishop for later.
Nf6 develops the king's knight and attacks the pawn on e4.

Be7 develops the dark-squared bishop and prepares castling.
Re1 puts the rook behind the pawn on e4.
b5 attacks the bishop on a4 and gains space.

Bd6 develops the dark-squared bishop and attacks the rook on e5. The rook should leave.
Re1 steps the rook off the bishop and back to the e-file.
Qh4 brings the queen out towards the king on g1. The attack has started.
g3 asks the queen a question and gives the king air. The pawn also blunts the bishop on d6.
Qh3 steps the queen off the pawn and attacks the pawn on h2.
Be3 develops the dark-squared bishop and covers the kingside.
Bg4 develops the light-squared bishop and attacks the queen on d1.
Qd3 steps the queen off the bishop and helps the defence.
Rae8 puts the other rook on the e-file. Both black rooks are now in the attack.
Nbd2 develops the queen's knight and defends the bishop on b3.

sib1.intro: The Najdorf, English Attack: Black kicks the knight with the e-pawn, the kings castle on opposite wings, and the pawn storms start on both sides.
notes: e4 opens the game and frees the light-squared bishop.
c5 fights for the centre from the flank.
Nf3 develops the king's knight and prepares to open the centre.

Nxd4 recaptures the pawn on d4. The knight sits in the centre.
Nf6 develops the king's knight and attacks the pawn on e4.
Nc3 develops the queen's knight and defends the pawn on e4.
a6 keeps a white piece off b5 and prepares expansion on the queenside.
Be3 develops the dark-squared bishop. White is building towards castling on the queenside.
e5 attacks the knight on d4 and gains space. The pawn on d6 stays back, which this line accepts.
Nb3 steps the knight off the pawn and leaves the dark-squared bishop on e3.
Be6 develops the light-squared bishop to an active square before the centre closes up.

Be7 develops the dark-squared bishop and prepares castling.
Qd2 develops the queen beside the bishop on e3 and prepares queenside castling.

Nbd7 develops the queen's knight without blocking the c-file.
g4 starts the pawn storm against the castled king.
b5 starts Black's own pawn storm on the queenside.

sib2.intro: The Najdorf against a bishop on g5. Black meets it with the e-pawn and the dark-squared bishop, the queen comes to c7, and the light-squared bishop lands on b7.
notes: e4 opens the game and frees the light-squared bishop. The queen's diagonal opens with it.
c5 fights for the centre from the flank and leaves the e-pawn at home.
Nf3 develops the king's knight and prepares to open the centre.
d6 keeps e5 under control and lets the king's knight come out.

cxd4 takes the pawn on d4 and opens the c-file. That file is where Black's counterplay lives.
Nxd4 recaptures the pawn on d4. The knight sits in the centre.
Nf6 develops the king's knight and attacks the pawn on e4.
Nc3 develops the queen's knight and defends the pawn on e4.
a6 keeps a white piece off b5. The pawn also prepares space on the queenside.
Bg5 develops the dark-squared bishop and attacks the knight on f6. The queen on d8 stands on that same diagonal.

Be7 develops the dark-squared bishop and defends the knight on f6. The bishop stands in front of the queen on d8, which is the solid choice here.
Qf3 develops the queen and defends the pawn on e4. She also defends the pawn on f4 and the knight on c3.
Qc7 develops the queen and attacks the knight on c3. The queen also defends the pawn on d6 and the bishop on e7.
O-O-O brings the king to c1 and the rook to d1. White castles long, with the rook on the half-open d-file.
Nbd7 develops the queen's knight and defends the knight on f6. The knight does not block the c-file.

Bb7 develops the light-squared bishop and attacks the pawn on e4. The bishop finishes development on the long diagonal.

sib3.intro: The Najdorf against a bishop on e2. Black kicks the knight with the e-pawn, both sides castle short, and the f-pawn is taken.
notes: e4 opens the game and frees the queen and the light-squared bishop.

Nxd4 recaptures the pawn on d4. White's knight occupies the square the pawn left.
Nf6 develops the king's knight and attacks the pawn on e4. Black starts to hit that pawn early.
Nc3 develops the queen's knight and defends the pawn on e4.
a6 takes b5 away from a white piece. Black keeps a flexible queenside.
Be2 develops the light-squared bishop and clears the king's path. It also attacks the pawn on a6.
e5 attacks the knight on d4 and gains space. The pawn on d6 stays back to hold the centre.

Nbd7 develops the queen's knight and defends the knight on f6. That is the knight the rook on f4 has just attacked.

sib4.intro: The Najdorf against a bishop on c4. The bishop drops back, both sides castle, and Black meets the f-pawn with queenside space and the light-squared bishop.
notes: e4 opens with a pawn in the centre and frees the light-squared bishop for an early diagonal.
c5 answers from the flank and leaves Black's e-pawn where it is.
Nf3 brings the king's knight towards the centre. White is ready to open the game.

d4 opens the centre at once and offers the pawn.

O-O brings the king to g1 and the rook to f1.

Bb7 develops the light-squared bishop and attacks the pawn on e4. The bishop takes the long diagonal.

sib8.intro: The Najdorf against an early a-pawn. Black kicks the knight, both sides castle, and the queen's knight comes to c6.
notes: e4 starts the game and frees the light-squared bishop.

notes: e4 opens the game. The light-squared bishop and the queen both gain a diagonal.
